description: Inspired by the Science Europe template for data management plans (Practical Guide to the International Alignment of Research Data Management): six core requirements with their guiding questions. Guidance is paraphrased; see https://scienceeurope.org/our-priorities/open-science/research-data-management/

sections.title: Administrative information
sections.content: Name of the applicant, project title, project number if known, funding programme and the version of this data management plan.

sections.title: 1. Data description and collection or re-use of existing data
1a. How will new data be collected or produced and/or how will existing data be re-used?
sections.content: Explain the methods, instruments or software used to create new data. For existing data, state where it comes from, any conditions on re-using it, and how its provenance will be recorded. If re-use was considered but rejected, say why.

sections.title: 1b. What data (for example the kind, formats, and volumes) will be collected or produced?
sections.content: Describe the kinds of data (numerical, text, images, audio, samples, ...), the file formats and the expected volume. Prefer open, widely used formats and justify any other choice.

sections.title: 2. Documentation and data quality
2a. What metadata and documentation will accompany the data?
sections.content: Name the metadata that will make the data understandable and findable, and any community metadata standard you will follow. Describe how files are organised (naming conventions, versioning, folder structure) and where the documentation lives, e.g. a README, a codebook or a lab notebook.

sections.title: 2b. What data quality control measures will be used?
sections.content: Describe how the consistency and quality of the data is checked and documented, for example calibration, repeated measurements, validation of data entry, controlled vocabularies or peer review.

sections.title: 3. Storage and backup during the research process
3a. How will data and metadata be stored and backed up during the research?
sections.content: Say where data is stored, how often it is backed up and to how many separate locations, who has access, and how data would be recovered after an incident. Managed institutional storage is preferred over laptops or portable drives.

sections.title: 3b. How will data security and protection of sensitive data be taken care of during the research?
sections.content: If the project handles sensitive data (personal, commercially or politically sensitive), describe the risks and the technical and organisational measures that address them, including relevant institutional policies.

sections.title: 4. Legal and ethical requirements, codes of conduct
4a. If personal data are processed, how will compliance with legislation on personal data and on security be ensured?
sections.content: Explain how the project complies with data protection law such as the GDPR: informed consent, anonymisation or pseudonymisation, encryption and separate key storage, and any controlled access procedure.

sections.title: 4b. How will other legal issues, such as intellectual property rights and ownership, be managed?
sections.content: State who owns the data, who controls access and under which licence it will be made available. Mention agreements between partners and any restrictions on re-using third-party data.

sections.title: 4c. What ethical issues and codes of conduct are there, and how will they be taken into account?
sections.content: Describe how ethical considerations affect storing, transferring, sharing and retaining the data, which codes of conduct apply, and whether an ethics review is required.

sections.title: 5. Data sharing and long-term preservation
5a. How and when will data be shared? Are there possible restrictions to data sharing or embargo reasons?
sections.content: Explain how others can discover and access the data, when it will be released, any embargo period, who may use it and under which conditions.

sections.title: 5b. How will data for preservation be selected, and where will data be preserved long-term?
sections.content: Describe which data must be kept or destroyed for legal or contractual reasons, how the remaining selection is made, how long data is retained, and which repository or archive will hold it.

sections.title: 5c. What methods or software tools are needed to access and use the data?
sections.content: State whether specialised software or tools are needed to use the data and how users will get access to them.

sections.title: 5d. How will the application of a unique and persistent identifier to each data set be ensured?
sections.content: Explain how datasets receive persistent identifiers such as DOIs, typically assigned by the repository, so they can be cited and found.

sections.title: 6. Data management responsibilities and resources
6a. Who will be responsible for data management?
sections.content: Name the roles (and people, where possible) responsible for data capture, metadata, quality, storage, archiving and sharing, how this is coordinated between partners, and who keeps this plan up to date.

sections.title: 6b. What resources will be dedicated to data management and ensuring that data will be FAIR?
sections.content: Estimate the time and costs of data management, such as storage, hardware, staff time and repository fees, and explain how they will be covered.
